Letter of November 1918, Collected Political Writings, 1921, p. 493.
Ahead of us lies “a polar night of icy darkness and hardness.”
“When this night slowly begins to lift, who will still be alive among those whose spring now seems to bloom so luxuriantly?”
“When the period of exhaustion is over, peace—not war—will have been discredited: a consequence of absolute ethics.”
“Anyone who wishes to act according to the ethics of the Gospel should, above all, not speak of revolution. Surely that ethics does not teach that civil war is the one and only legitimate war.”
Once war is no longer legal and legal wars come to an end, legitimate wars begin!
How could I have allowed myself to be annoyed for even a second by Hans Barth’s petty human subordination and his article on Leviathan?
Among the shadows cast by the name Leviathan, one of which falls across my little book, there is also this touching little darkener.
He too eagerly carries over his tiny piece of blackout equipment, just as the old woman carried her piece of wood to the pyre of Jan Hus. So here too, in response to the Neue Zürcher Zeitung:
Let us not deprive the old woman of what gives her inner support, nor Mr Barth of his moral foundation.
Let him keep the background against which he defines himself through us Germans.
How unbearable I found the polished, self-righteous tone in which Fritz Ernst spoke about his fellow Swiss, the statesman and historian Johannes Müller (Corona VII, 1937).
And yet that essay contained the wonderful sentence, concerning Johannes von Müller’s conflict with Jérôme in May 1809:
“No one knows in advance what he is capable of carrying, or what he will be willing to endure. The decision belongs to the mystery of the incalculable moment.”
How does a Swiss know things so true? And why does he refuse to let them apply to us? Or is this kind of generosity and wisdom merely an internal Swiss ethic that does not apply to Germans?
Under the influence of Barion’s letter of 11 November, I feel a strong temptation to write a continuation of B.[enito] C.[ereno] on another level:
Perhaps its mood could be combined with elements from Franz Kafka’s novel The Trial.
Is this how B. C. should end?
B. C. charged with piracy before a court that refuses to permit any discussion of the “foundations” on which the case itself rests.
Will he step onto this carpet woven out of concepts?
The problem of every political trial?
Before an admiralty court, he has a chance.
Before a special tribunal created to combat Spanish imperialism, he has none.
Magnificent, Aldous Huxley’s comment in Time Must Have a Stop on the dying Hotspur’s lines from Henry IV, Part One, Act V:
Thought is the slave of life; life is time’s fool; and time, which surveys the whole world, must one day stop.
Thought is the servant of life. But that philosophy of life is only the first sentence.
The thought continues: life itself is the fool of time. And time itself eventually ends.
Why should I not surrender myself to the comfort of these lines and to the Patinir-blue gentleness of this Advent evening?
I am not, after all, the owner of possessions belonging to this life whose servant my thought would then be. I have no possessions. I have only a domain: as far as my eye and my thought can reach.
Others possess the domain of the hands, the manus.
I recognized myself and my own way of thinking in every sentence of Aldous Huxley.
Certainly more than an exchange of letters.
Only do not try to turn your thinking into a possession.
Popitz’s birthday. This Prussian civil servant had something of Thomas More about him.
More too possessed the humanist gift for friendship.
Popitz could never have written a Utopia. But perhaps he could have invented one.
For that very reason, he himself could never afterward have written “utopias” in the ordinary sense.
Machiavelli could never have been a Machiavellian.
People of the Thomas More type no longer write utopias today. What did Popitz invent?

No new literary genre, because he was not a man of letters. But he had something of Thomas More’s humanist holiness. He did not push himself toward martyrdom. He gave way for as long as giving way was possible. And when death became unavoidable, he remained cheerful.
Speaking of the title of Annie Kraus’s essay, I am reminded that an acquaintance of hers, Dr R., appeared in Berlin in April while I was still imprisoned and tore me to pieces.
But you know, Paul Adams, that I have never been one to spoil another man’s fun. So let us not disturb him further in the enjoyment of his satisfactions.
A true Brahmin feels pity for the tiger that eats him. And a true sociologist feels understanding—or rather, “understands”—the proscription lists on which his own name appears.
And now I am reading in Baader that it can be proved to every human being that his greatest pleasure, even the worst one, is ultimately nothing more than an answered prayer.
Strange protective masks are growing inside us, allowing us to pass through Advent undisturbed.
Today every physicist knows what in earlier times was clear only to good theorists of knowledge: the object being observed is changed by the very act of observing it.

If that already applies to observation conducted with the exact methods of natural science, how much more must it apply to the kind of observation through which a trial court establishes the facts of a case: through questioning witnesses, statements by the parties, open or unspoken presumptions, and the assumed “foundations” of the trial itself, which no one is permitted to discuss.
The changes made to the object, the distortions of perspective created by the forms of the trial, must then become enormous.
In abnormal times, dealing with abnormal events, the result can only be falsification. It becomes worst of all when amnesty does not arrive in time.
The judge does not concern himself with the smallest things.
Maxima non curat praetor. Nor with the greatest things.
Not too small and not too large.
Above all: not too high and not too deep, not too near and not too far. Here too, in everything: the “middle.”
Law exists only in the right place.

Why are the classes moyennes, the middle classes, the true sociological home of jurists? What is the sociological home of the theologians of Scholasticism? And what, therefore, did the removal of theology from legal science mean—especially in international law?
Endlessly stirring up the rubbish bin again.
German pedantry as an obstacle to every reasonable amnesty.
At bottom, none of this interests either victor or defeated. It interests only that third person who is both involved and uninvolved and wants to enjoy his entirely personal revenge.
Amnesty too belongs to the primal foundations of anything that can properly be called law.

The dissolution and abolition of thing-like reality is at the same time the abolition of what has been posited and of law itself—which are the same thing—and the transformation of the world into pure action.
The concept of genius is the great disaster.
Most revealing of all—most brilliant about brilliance—is Kierkegaard-Haufniensis in The Concept of Anxiety, pp. 97–100.
O God, all these brilliant arch-priests of the primal I that does nothing but act, that consists of nothing but activity.
The “primal positions” contain the essence of finite things (!) in an eternal form. They make up the ideal material from which God created the world. Thus Böhme, Fichte, and so on.
In criminalization there is a mismatch within the legal definition of the factual offence:
“war of aggression” is therefore the condition for making the legal consequences indefinite.
The “outlawing” of “war” replaces the atavism of war with the atavism of outlawry!
